The conceptions are moulded in a form peculiarly adapted to Nebuchadnezzar's modes of thought.<div eID="gen21726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the living--</hi>not as distinguished from the dead, but from the inhabitants of heaven, who "know" that which the men of the world need to the taught (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Psa 9:16</reference>); the ungodly confess there is a God, but would gladly confine Him to heaven. But, saith Daniel, God ruleth not merely there, but "in the kingdom of men."<div eID="gen21727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">basest--</hi>the lowest in condition (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1Sa 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.52">Lu 1:52</reference>). It is not one's talents, excellency, or noble birth, but God's will, which elevates to the throne. Nebuchadnezzar abased to the dunghill, and then restored, was to have in himself an experimental proof of this (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.37">Da 4:37</reference>). <div eID="gen21728" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c457f85cdd5f1e6304a87fda4f2dcee3c40330b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12024"/><div sID="gen21729" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12024"/><hi type="bold">19. Daniel ... Belteshazzar--</hi>The use of the Hebrew as well as the Chaldee name, so far from being an objection, as some have made it, is an undesigned mark of genuineness. In a proclamation to "all people," and one designed to honor the God of the Hebrews, Nebuchadnezzar would naturally use the Hebrew name (derived from El, "God," the name by which the prophet was best known among his countrymen), as well as the Gentile name by which he was known in the Chaldean empire.<div eID="gen21729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">astonied--</hi>overwhelmed with awe at the terrible import of the dream.<div eID="gen21730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one hour--</hi>the original means often "a moment," or "short time," as in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.6">Da 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.15">15</reference>.<div eID="gen21731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21732" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let not the dream ... trouble thee--</hi>Many despots would have punished a prophet who dared to foretell his overthrow. Nebuchadnezzar assures Daniel he may freely speak out.<div eID="gen21732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the dream be to them that hate thee--</hi>We are to desire the prosperity of those under whose authority God's providence has placed us (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.7">Jr 29:7</reference>). The wish here is not so much against others, as for the king: a common formula (<reference osisRef="2Sam.18.32">2Sa 18:32</reference>). It is not the language of uncharitable hatred. <div eID="gen21733" type="x-p"/>
entries.363b6e1ddf4c005bc5902809bd1fc52af7d57218: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12025"/><div sID="gen21734" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12025"/>20. The tree is the king. The branches, the princes. The leaves, the soldiers. The fruits, the revenues. The shadow, the protection afforded to dependent states. <div eID="gen21734" type="x-p"/>
entries.8128b40a06cd10e446a0f4ec86105fdedcb8781f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12026"/><div sID="gen21735" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12026"/><hi type="bold">22. It is thou--</hi>He speaks pointedly, and without circumlocution (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.7">2Sa 12:7</reference>). While pitying the king, he uncompromisingly pronounces his sentence of punishment. Let ministers steer the mean between, on the one hand, fulminations against sinners under the pretext of zeal, without any symptom of compassion; and, on the other, flattery of sinners under the pretext of moderation.<div eID="gen21735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21736" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the end of the earth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.27.6-Jer.27.8">Jr 27:6-8</reference>). To the Caspian, Euxine, and Atlantic seas. <div eID="gen21736" type="x-p"/>
entries.9216680c30fe68a4393863f5f8ee01a2a6b7fe03: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12027"/><div sID="gen21737" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12027"/><hi type="bold">24. decree of the Most High--</hi>What was termed in <reference osisRef="Dan.4.17">Da 4:17</reference> by Nebuchadnezzar, "the decree of the watchers," is here more accurately termed by Daniel, "the decree of the Most High." They are but His ministers. <div eID="gen21737" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3771bbdb1b52c6a3898b8db51baccd58af9e317: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12028"/><div sID="gen21738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12028"/><hi type="bold">25. they shall drive thee--</hi>a Chaldee idiom for "thou shalt be driven." Hypochondriacal madness was his malady, which "drove" him under the fancy that he was a beast, to "dwell with the beasts"; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.34">Da 4:34</reference> proves this, "mine understanding returned." The regency would leave him to roam in the large beast-abounding parks attached to the palace.<div eID="gen21738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat grass--</hi>that is, vegetables, or herbs in general (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.18">Ge 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen21739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall wet thee--</hi>that is, thou shalt be wet.<div eID="gen21740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21741" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">till thou know, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.83.17">Psa 83:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.5">Jr 27:5</reference>). <div eID="gen21741" type="x-p"/>
entries.47cb955817064dd3a8aead11ff5de6fcee3693e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12029"/><div sID="gen21742" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12029"/><hi type="bold">26. thou shalt have known, &c.--</hi>a promise of spiritual grace to him, causing the judgment to humble, not harden, his heart.<div eID="gen21742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heavens do rule--</hi>The plural is used, as addressed to Nebuchadnezzar, the head of an organized earthly kingdom, with various principalities under the supreme ruler. So "the kingdom of heaven" (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.17">Mt 4:17</reference>; Greek, "kingdom of the heavens") is a manifold organization, composed of various orders of angels, under the Most High (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.20">Ep 1:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.10">3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col 1:16</reference>). <div eID="gen21743" type="x-p"/>
entries.49fda312f25b79eee8f5d8e7888ceebd0a846588: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12030"/><div sID="gen21744" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12030"/><hi type="bold">27. break off--</hi>as a galling yoke (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.40">Ge 27:40</reference>); sin is a heavy load (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Mt 11:28</reference>). The Septuagint and Vulgate translate not so well, "redeem," which is made an argument for Rome's doctrine of the expiation of sins by meritorious works. Even translate it so, it can only mean; Repent and show the reality of thy repentance by works of justice and charity (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.11.41">Lu 11:41</reference>); so God will remit thy punishment. The trouble will be longer before it comes, or shorter when it does come. Compare the cases of Hezekiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.1-Isa.38.5">Is 38:1-5</reference>; Nineveh, <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.5-Jonah.3.10">Jon 3:5-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.7">Jr 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.8">8</reference>. The change is not in God, but in the sinner who repents. As the king who had provoked God's judgments by sin, so he might avert it by a return to righteousness (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.41.1">Psa 41:1</reference>, 2; <reference osisRef="Acts.8.22">Ac 8:22</reference>). Probably, like most Oriental despots, Nebuchadnezzar had oppressed the poor by forcing them to labor in his great public works without adequate remuneration.<div eID="gen21744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if ... lengthening of ... tranquillity--</hi>if haply thy present prosperity shall be prolonged. <div eID="gen21745" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fc7032b1fbfe9ebfaef503e107e3703fae373e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12031"/><div sID="gen21746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12031"/><hi type="bold">29. twelve months--</hi>This respite was granted to him to leave him without excuse. So the hundred twenty years granted before the flood (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Ge 6:3</reference>). At the first announcement of the coming judgment he was alarmed, as Ahab (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.27">1Ki 21:27</reference>), but did not thoroughly repent; so when judgment was not executed at once, he thought it would never come, and so returned to his former pride (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Ec 8:11</reference>).<div eID="gen21746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the palace--</hi>rather, upon the (flat) palace roof, whence he could contemplate the splendor of Babylon. So the heathen historian, Abydenus, records. The palace roof was the scene of the fall of another king (<reference osisRef="2Sam.11.2">2Sa 11:2</reference>). The outer wall of Nebuchadnezzar's new palace embraced six miles; there were two other embattled walls within, and a great tower, and three brazen gates. <div eID="gen21747" type="x-p"/>
entries.52e0784e257922549db912f54fb333c709d683ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12032"/><div sID="gen21748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12032"/><hi type="bold">30. Babylon, that I have built--</hi>Herodotus ascribes the building of Babylon to Semiramis and Nitocris, his informant under the Persian dynasty giving him the Assyrian and Persian account. Berosus and Abydenus give the Babylonian account, namely, that Nebuchadnezzar added much to the old city, built a splendid palace and city walls. Herodotus, the so-called "father of history," does not even mention Nebuchadnezzar. (Nitocris, to whom he attributes the beautifying of Babylon, seems to have been Nebuchadnezzar's wife). Hence infidels have doubted the Scripture account. But the latter is proved by thousands of bricks on the plain, the inscriptions of which have been deciphered, each marked "Nebuchadnezzar, the son of Nabopolassar." "Built," that is, restored and enlarged (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.5">2Ch 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.6">6</reference>). It is curious, all the bricks have been found with the stamped face downwards. Scarcely a figure in stone, or tablet, has been dug out of the rubbish heaps of Babylon, whereas Nineveh abounds in them; fulfilling <reference osisRef="Jer.51.37">Jr 51:37</reference>, "Babylon shall become heaps." The "I" is emphatic, by which he puts himself in the place of God; so the "my ... my." He impiously opposes his might to God's, as though God's threat, uttered a year before, could never come to pass. He would be more than man; God, therefore, justly, makes him less than man. An acting over again of the fall; Adam, once lord of the world and the very beasts (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.28">Ge 1:28</reference>; so Nebuchadnezzar <reference osisRef="Dan.2.38">Da 2:38</reference>), would be a god (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.5">Ge 3:5</reference>); therefore he must die like the beasts (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.6">Psa 82:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.12">49:12</reference>). The second Adam restores the forfeited inheritance (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.4-Ps.8.8">Psa 8:4-8</reference>). <div eID="gen21748" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e1479b946a27c4599d046d3fcdd995c5ee547da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12033"/><div sID="gen21749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12033"/><hi type="bold">31. While, &c.--</hi>in the very act of speaking, so that there could be no doubt as to the connection between the crime and the punishment. So <reference osisRef="Luke.12.19">Lu 12:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">20</reference>.<div eID="gen21749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">O king ... to thee it is spoken--</hi>Notwithstanding thy kingly power, to thee thy doom is now spoken, there is to be no further respite. <div eID="gen21750" type="x-p"/>
entries.e29c53e659f750599c3590dd7bde3f5def703a50: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12034"/><div sID="gen21751" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12034"/><hi type="bold">33. driven from men--</hi>as a maniac fancying himself a wild beast. It is possible, a conspiracy of his nobles may have co-operated towards his having been "driven" forth as an outcast.<div eID="gen21751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hairs ... eagles' feathers--</hi>matted together, as the hair-like, thick plumage of the ossifraga eagle. The "nails," by being left uncut for years, would become like "claws." <div eID="gen21752" type="x-p"/>
entries.9390d64f2d50dfcfa04b1fdbde90b693154172d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12035"/><div sID="gen21753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12035"/><hi type="bold">34. lifted up mine eyes unto heaven--</hi>whence the "voice" had issued (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.31">Da 4:31</reference>) at the beginning of his visitation. Sudden mental derangement often has the effect of annihilating the whole interval, so that, when reason returns, the patient remembers only the event that immediately preceded his insanity. Nebuchadnezzar's looking up towards heaven was the first symptom of his "understanding" having "returned." Before, like the beasts, his eyes had been downward to the earth. Now, like Jonah's (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.1">Jon 2:1</reference>, 2, 4) out of the fish's belly, they are lifted up to heaven in prayer. He turns to Him that smiteth him (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Is 9:13</reference>), with the faint glimmer of reason left to him, and owns God's justice in punishing him.<div eID="gen21753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21754" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">praised ... him--</hi>Praise is a sure sign of a soul spiritually healed (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.12">Psa 116:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.5.15">Mr 5:15</reference>, 18, 19).<div eID="gen21754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ... honoured him--</hi>implying that the cause of his chastisement was that he had before robbed God of His honor.<div eID="gen21755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting dominion--</hi>not temporary or mutable, as a human king's dominion. <div eID="gen21756" type="x-p"/>
entries.cbbe46c34e742c674f34903537af47cd27cad931: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12036"/><div sID="gen21757" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12036"/><hi type="bold">35. all ... as nothing--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.40.15">Is 40:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen21757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to his will in ... heaven--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.115.3">Psa 115:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.135.6">135:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.10">Mt 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Ep 1:11</reference>).<div eID="gen21758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">army--</hi>the heavenly hosts, angels and starry orbs (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.24.21">Is 24:21</reference>).<div eID="gen21759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none ... stay his hand--</hi>literally, "strike His hand." Image from striking the hand of another, to check him in doing anything (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.13">Is 43:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">45:9</reference>).<div eID="gen21760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">What doest thou--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.9.12">Job 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.20">Ro 9:20</reference>). <div eID="gen21761" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a5ff8029aa53ed813f1c0a512e64d79378bc26b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12037"/><div sID="gen21762" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12037"/>36. An inscription in the East India Company's Museum is read as describing the period of Nebuchadnezzar's insanity [G. V. Smith]. In the so-called standard inscription read by Sir H. Rawlinson, Nebuchadnezzar relates that during four (?) years he ceased to lay out buildings, or to furnish with victims Merodach's altar, or to clear out the canals for irrigation. No other instance in the cuneiform inscriptions occurs of a king recording his own inaction.<div eID="gen21762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21763" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my counsellors ... sought unto me--</hi>desired to have me, as formerly, to be their head, wearied with the anarchy which prevailed in my absence (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Dan.4.33">Da 4:33</reference>); the likelihood of a conspiracy of the nobles is confirmed by this verse.<div eID="gen21763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">majesty was added--</hi>My authority was greater than ever before (<reference osisRef="Job.42.12">Job 42:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.4">Pr 22:4</reference>; "added," <reference osisRef="Matt.6.33">Mt 6:33</reference>). <div eID="gen21764" type="x-p"/>
entries.053267c49bd20706c64e18ba10c113a907bc48d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12038"/><div sID="gen21765" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12038"/><hi type="bold">37. praise ... extol ... honour--</hi>He heaps word on word, as if he cannot say enough in praise of God.<div eID="gen21765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all whose works ... truth ... judgment--</hi>that is, are true and just (<reference osisRef="Rev.15.3">Re 15:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.16.7">16:7</reference>). God has not dealt unjustly or too severely with me; whatever I have suffered, I deserved it all. It is a mark of true contrition to condemn one's self, and justify God (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Psa 51:4</reference>).<div eID="gen21766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">those that walk in pride ... abase--</hi>exemplified in me. He condemns himself before the whole world, in order to glorify God. <chapter eID="Dan.4"/>

entries.59a4de69fc6a2d7fb36460fab2196a3b7297bac4: <div eID="gen32963" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32964" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32965" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32965" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32964" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32966" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar, after having subdued all the neighboring countries, and greatly enriched and adorned his own, became so intoxicated with his prosperity, as to draw down upon himself a very remarkable judgment, of which this chapter gives a particular account, in the very words of the edict or proclamation which the Babylonish monarch issued on his restoration to the throne. This state document begins with Nebuchadnezzar's acknowledging the hand of God in his late malady, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.1-Dan.4.3">Dan 4:1-3</reference>. It then gives an account of the dream of Nebuchadnezzar, which portended the loss of his kingdom and reason for seven years, on account of his pride and arrogance, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.4-Dan.4.18">Dan 4:4-18</reference>. So it was explained by Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.19-Dan.4.27">Dan 4:19-27</reference>, and so it was verified by the event, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.28-Dan.4.33">Dan 4:28-33</reference>. It then recites how, at the end of the period fixed by the God of heaven for the duration of his malady, the Chaldean monarch became sensible of his dependence on the Supreme Being, and lifted up has eyes to heaven in devout acknowledgment of the sovereign majesty of the King of kings, the Ruler of the earth, whose dominion alone is universal, unchangeable, and everlasting, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.34-Dan.4.37">Dan 4:34-37</reference>. <div eID="gen32966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32967" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32968" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar the king, unto all people - This is a regular decree, and is one of the most ancient on record; and no doubt was copied from the state papers of Babylon. Daniel has preserved it in the original language.
entries.dd4ac53f93b064eef74e8471a79a1b8e230f69a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32969" type="x-p"/> I thought it good to show - A part of the decree was a recital of the wonders wrought by the hand of the true God in his kingdom and on his person.
entries.a27b4fa888c7c41de1b8fa11af730f05c46970be: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen32969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32970" type="x-p"/> How great are his signs! - There are no preternatural signs like his! His wonders - miraculous interferences, are mighty - they surpass all human power. He is the Sovereign of all kings, and his dominion is everlasting; and every generation is a proof of his all-governing influence. These are very fine sentiments, and show how deeply his mind was impressed with the majesty of God.
entries.fe37d4522ab5a8be715b8a4500288ffa12c8a570: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen32970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32971" type="x-p"/> I - was at rest - I had returned to my palace in Babylon after having subdued Syria, Phoenicia, Judea, Egypt, and Arabia. It was probably these great conquests that puffed him up with pride, and brought that chastisement upon him which he afterwards describes. See the dream of the emblematical tree explained.
entries.a3958a9548d197c9423b86624bbe9c0ab0e276b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32972" type="x-p"/> I saw a dream - See this dream circumstantially explained in the following verses.
entries.7e2f36c72a599f3c8a301fecca7dd4e7c0007899: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen32972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32973" type="x-p"/> I saw - a tree - This vision Nebuchadnezzar says made him afraid. What a mercy it is that God has hidden futurity from us! Were he to show every man the lot that is before him, the misery of the human race would be complete. <div eID="gen32973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32974" type="x-p"/> Great men and princes are often represented, in the language of the prophets, under the similitude of trees; see <reference osisRef="Eze.17.5">Eze 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.17.6">Eze 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.31.3">Eze 31:3</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">Jer 22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.1.3">Psa 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.37.35">Psa 37:35</reference>.
entries.d1e7949db2c8cfad3e1ec60117cb5a4590ba0c55: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen32974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32975" type="x-p"/> A watcher and a holy one - These are both angels; but, according to the Chaldean oracles, of different orders. They appear, according to their opinions, to be a kind of judges of human actions who had the power of determining the lot of men; see <reference osisRef="Dan.4.17">Dan 4:17</reference>.
entries.f6455ef669ccf4bc656ff1a38a4b5470a04a805d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen32975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32976" type="x-p"/> Hew down the tree - As the tree was to be cut down, the beasts are commanded to flee away from under his branches. His courtiers, officers, etc., all abandoned him as soon as his insanity appeared; but he soon fled from the society of men.
entries.afd68c4b98ebab4fea384863266d6134613ceaf7: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen32976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32977" type="x-p"/> Leave the stump - Let him not be destroyed, nor his kingdom alienated.
entries.b11186870ea65d44fe52a01659115390efda2d7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen32977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32978" type="x-p"/> Let his heart be changed - Let him conceive himself to be a beast, and act as such, herding among the beasts of the field. <div eID="gen32978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32979" type="x-p"/> Let seven times pass over him - Let him continue in this state for seven years. I knew a man who was thus changed in his heart - in his imagination. He believed himself to be a bear, and would imitate the ursal growl, etc.; and the case did not appear to be hypochondriacal. Whether he ever came to sound mind, I know not.
entries.4782c7a13bb3f4138e49c76573cb190f832f3ecd: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32980" type="x-p"/> This matter is by the decree of the watchers - See on <reference osisRef="Dan.4.13">Dan 4:13</reference> (note). <div eID="gen32980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32981" type="x-p"/> The Most High ruleth - He never leaves the government of the world to man, to second causes, or to fortuitous occurrences. What are thus called are his agents; they are no moving causes. <div eID="gen32981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32982" type="x-p"/> And setteth up - the basest of men - "Tyrants and kings from Jove proceed <div eID="gen32982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32983" type="x-p"/> Those are permitted, these decreed." <div eID="gen32983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32984" type="x-p"/> The throne ennobles no man: to be properly filled, the man must be noble. Some of the greatest and some of the meanest of men have sat on the throne. Kings differ in education, seldom in intellect, from the common mass of men; the power and authority are from God. The king himself may be given either in mercy or in wrath. When James II ruled this kingdom, it might well be said, God hath set up over it the basest of men. His successor was one of the best. The former nearly ruined it both in a civil and religious point of view; the latter was the means of restoring it in both these respects.
entries.381ede80efad9278dc632c814a1870d05727c53d: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen32984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32985" type="x-p"/> Daniel - was astonied for one hour - He saw the design of the dream, and he felt the great delicacy of interpreting it. He was not puzzled by the difficulties of it. He felt for the king, and for the nation; and with what force and delicacy does he express the general portent; "The dream to them that hate thee, and the interpretation thereof to thine enemies!"
entries.47187d55f4f4ca636cf39af02a937a2dba4c7f52: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen32985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32986" type="x-p"/> The tree that thou sawest - The dream is so fully interpreted in the following verses that it needs no comment.
entries.af0e870275fc069bb706be8bbaae8f074b7668a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen32986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32987" type="x-p"/> Thy kingdom shall he sure unto thee - No new king was set up; Evil-merodach his son was regent during his father's insanity.
entries.c57a8623bc902b1e7d519de731601f1d1512f831: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen32987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32988" type="x-p"/> Break off thy sins by righteousness - Do justice. Thou hast been an oppressive man; show mercy to the poor, many of whom have been made such by thyself: witness the whole nation of the Jews. He was to cease from his sins - repent and bring forth fruits meet for repentance, in order that he might find mercy at the hand of God.
entries.bbbca5cc9659e4953548070f951e1d882cc4b837: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen32988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32989" type="x-p"/> Is not this great Babylon - Here his heart was inflated with pride; he attributed every thing to himself, and acknowledged God in nothing. The walls, hanging gardens, temple of Bel, and the royal palace, all built by Nebuchadnezzar, made it the greatest city in the world.
entries.62d223b74514d50faa3b373b33b402ae7e2a6748: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen32989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32990" type="x-p"/> While the word was in the king's mouth - How awful to a victorious and proud king: "Thy kingdom is departed from thee!" All thy goods and gods are gone in a moment!
entries.7b3657d18ef999f04b24952713084edf2ef1fdfb: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen32990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32991" type="x-p"/> They shall make thee, etc. - Thou shalt be made to eat grass as oxen. The madness that fell upon him induced him to forsake society, and to run to the woods and deserts, where he lived like a wild beast, his hairs growing long and thick, so as to be a substitute for clothing; and his nails strong and hooked, that he might the better climb trees and grub up the ground, in order to get roots and earth-nuts. It was the mercy of God that thus clothed and accoutred him. His case seems much like that of the maniac in the Gospel, whose dwelling was among the tombs and in the mountains, and who shunned the society of men.
entries.40c98188f748b1cb9f9c420ef38af2026979ca1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen32991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32992" type="x-p"/> My reason returned - Every thing was fulfilled that was exhibited by the dream and its interpretation. It is very likely that this unfortunate king had so concealed himself that the place of his retreat was not found out; and the providence of God had so watched over every thing, that, on his return to his palace, he found his counselors and his lords, who received him gladly, and cleaved to and served him as they had formerly done.
entries.bd464b272dc38b4355f88fd564af88cfbd857552: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen32992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32993" type="x-p"/> Now I - praise and extol - It is very probable that Nebuchadnezzar was a true convert; that he relapsed no more into idolatry, and died in the faith of the God of Israel. It is supposed that he lived seventeen years after his restoration. But the authorized Version, which is followed in the margin, states the date of this decree to be b.c. 563, the year preceding Nebuchadnezzar's death.  <chapter eID="Dan.4"/> <div eID="gen32993" type="x-p"/>

entries.b27706cd31abaf29efc7762f49df929c64c630fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9"/><title type="x-s">These verses form the introduction<note placement="foot">The connection of these verses with the third chapter in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin Bibles is altogether improper. The originator of the division into chapters appears to have entertained the idea that Nebuchadnezzar had made known the miracle of the deliverance of the three men from the fiery furnace to his subjects by means of a proclamation, according to which the fourth chapter would contain a new royal proclamation different from that former one, - an idea which was rejected by Luther, who has accordingly properly divided the chapters. Conformably to that division, as Chr. B. Michaelis has well remarked, “<hi type="italic">prius illud programma in fine capitis tertii excerptum caput sine corpore, posterius vero quod capite IV exhibetur, corpus sine capite, illic enim conspicitur quidem exordium, sed sine narratione, hic vero narratio quidem, sed sine exordio</hi>.” Quite arbitrarily Ewald has, according to the lxx, who have introduced the words  ̓Αρχὴ τῆς ἐπιστολης͂ before Daniel 3:31, and  ̓Ετους ὀκτωκαιδεκάτου τῆς βασλείας Ναβουχοδονόσορ ει before <reference osisRef="Dan.4.1">Dan 4:1</reference>, enlarged this passage by the superscription: “In the 28th year of the reign of king Nebuchadnezzar, king Nebuchadnezzar wrote thus to all the nations, communities, and tongues who dwell in the whole earth.”</note> to the manifesto, and consist of the expression of good wishes, and the announcement of its object. The mode of address here used, accompanied by an expression of a good wish, is the usual form also of the edicts promulgated by the Persian kings; cf. Ezr 4:17; Ezr 7:12. Regarding the designation of his subjects, cf. Dan 3:4. בּכל-ארעא, not “in all lands” (Häv.), but <hi type="italic">on the whole earth</hi>, for Nebuchadnezzar regarded himself as the lord of the whole earth. ותמהיּא אתיּא corresponds with the Hebr. וּמפתים אותת; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.6.22">Deu 6:22</reference>; Deu 7:19. The experience of this miracle leads to the offering up of praise to God, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.33">Dan 4:33</reference> (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.3">Daniel 4:3</reference>). The doxology of the second part of <reference osisRef="Dan.4.33">Dan 4:33</reference> occurs again with little variation in <reference osisRef="Dan.4.31">Daniel 4:31</reference> (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.34">Dan 4:34</reference>), <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Dan 7:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.18">Dan 7:18</reference>, and is met with also in <reference osisRef="Ps.145.13">Psa 145:13</reference>, which bears the name of David; while the rendering of עם־דּר , <hi type="italic">from generation to generation</hi>, i.e., as long as generations exist, agrees with Psa 72:5.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9"/><reference osisRef="Dan.4.4">Dan 4:4</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:1) <div sID="gen15582" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Dan.4.1">Daniel 4:1</reference> (v. 4) Nebuchadnezzar begins the narration of his wonderful experience. When he was at rest in his palace and prospering, he had a dream as he lay upon his bed which made him afraid and perplexed. שׁלה, <hi type="italic">quiet, in undisturbed, secure prosperity</hi>. רענן, properly <hi type="italic">growing green</hi>, of the fresh, vigorous growth of a tree, to which the happiness and prosperity of men are often compared; e.g., in Ps. 52:10 (8), <reference osisRef="Ps.92.12">Psa 92:12</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.10">10</reference>). Here plainly the word is chosen with reference to the tree which had been seen in the dream. From this description of his prosperity it appears that after his victories Nebuchadnezzar enjoyed the fruit of his exploits, was firmly established on his throne, and, as appears from v. 26 (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.29">Dan 4:29</reference>)f., a year after his dream could look with pleasure and pride on the completion of his splendid buildings in Babylon; and therefore this event belongs to the last half of his reign.
entries.6cf6e372553e0f4f8db6c6f055e2717ebf3a390a: <reference osisRef="Dan.4.5">Dan 4:5</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:2) <div eID="gen15582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15583" type="x-p"/> While in this state of security and peace, he was alarmed by a dream. The abrupt manner in which the matter is here introduced well illustrates the unexpected suddenness of the even itself. הרהרין, <hi type="italic">thoughts</hi>, from הרהר, <hi type="italic">to think, to meditate</hi>; in the Mishna and in Syr. <hi type="italic">images of the imagination</hi>; here, <hi type="italic">images in a dream</hi>. The words משׁכּבי על הרהרין are more properly taken as a passage by themselves with the verb, I had (I saw), supplied, than connected with the following noun to יבהלנּני. Regarding ראשׁי חזוי see under Dan 2:28. On this matter Chr. B. Michaelis has well remarked: ”<hi type="italic">Licet somnii interpretationem nondum intelligeret, tamen sensit, infortunium sibi isthoc somnio portendi.”</hi>
entries.51357d5cc07af5571d9f5c1d886e87e2a62ae306: <reference osisRef="Dan.4.6-Dan.4.9">Dan 4:6-9</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:3-6) <div eID="gen15583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15584" type="x-p"/> Therefore Nebuchadnezzar commanded the wise men of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.2">Dan 2:2</reference>) to be called to him, that they might interpret to him the dream. But they could not do so, although on this occasion he only asked them to give the interpretation, and not, as in <reference osisRef="Dan.2.2">Dan 2:2</reference>, at the same time the dream itself. Instead of the <hi type="italic">Kethiv</hi> עללין, the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> here and at <reference osisRef="Dan.5.8">Dan 5:8</reference> gives the contracted form עלּין, which became possible only by the shortening of , as in חשׁחן Dan 3:16. The form אחרין is differently explained; apparently it must be the <hi type="italic">plur. masc.</hi> instead of אחרן, and אחרין עד, <hi type="italic">to the last</hi>, a circumlocution of the adverb <hi type="italic">at last</hi>. That אחרין means <hi type="italic">posterus</hi>, and אחרן <hi type="italic">alius</hi>, Hitzig has not yet furnished the proof. The question, wherefore Daniel came only when the Chaldean wise men could not interpret the dream, is not answered satisfactorily by the remark of Zündel, p. 16, that it was the natural course that first they should be called who by virtue of their wisdom should interpret the dream, and that then, after their wisdom had failed, Daniel should be called, who had gained for himself a name by revelations not proceeding from the class of the Magi. For if Nebuchadnezzar had still the events of Daniel 2 in view, he would without doubt have called him forthwith, since it certainly did not come into his mind, in his anxiety on account of his dream, first to try the natural wisdom of his Magi. The objection offered by Hitzig, that the king does not go at once to his chief magician, v. 6 (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.9">Dan 4:9</reference>), who had already (Daniel 2) shown himself to be the best interpreter of dreams, is not thereby confuted; still less is it by the answer that the custom was not immediately to call the president of the Magi (Jahn), or that in the haste he was not at once thought of (Häv.). Though it may have been the custom not to call the chief president in every particular case, yet a dream by the king, which had filled him with terror, was an altogether unusual occurrence. If Daniel, therefore, was in this case first called only when the natural wisdom of the Magi had proved its inadequacy, the reason of this was, either that Nebuchadnezzar had forgotten what had occurred several years before (Daniel 2), and since the chief president of the wise men was only in special cases called on for counsel, therefore only the incorporated cultivators of the magician’s art were called, and only when these could not accomplish that which was asked of them was the chief president Daniel required to come, - or it lay in this, that the king, afraid of receiving an unwelcome answer, purposely adopted the course indicated. Kranichfeld has decided in favour of this latter supposition. <hi type="italic">“</hi>The king,” he thinks, “knew from the dream itself that the tree (v. 8 [Dan 4:11]) reaching unto heaven and extending to the end of the whole earth represented a royal person ruling the earth, who could come to ruin <hi type="italic">on account of the God of the Jews</hi>, and would remain in his ruin till there was an acknowledgment of the Almighty; cf. vv. 13, 14, (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Dan 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.17">Dan 4:17</reference>). There was this reason for the king’s keeping Daniel the Jew at a distance from this matter of the dream. Without doubt he would think himself intended by the person concerned in the dream; and since the special direction which the dream took (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.14">Dan 4:14</reference>) set forth as its natural point of departure an actual relation corresponding to that of the king to the God of Daniel, it must have occasioned to him a well-grounded fear (cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.4.24">Dan 4:24</reference>), as in the case of Ahab, the idolater, towards Micah, the prophet of Jehovah (cf. 1Ki 22:8), of a severe judgment, leading him to treat with any other regarding his matter rather than with Daniel.” For the establishment of this view Kranichfeld refers to the “king’s subsequent address to Daniel, designed especially to appease and captivate (vv. 5, 6 [Dan 4:8, Dan 4:9]), as well as the visibly mild and gentle deportment of the king toward the worshipper of the God of the Jews.” This proceeding tending to captivate appears in the appellation, <hi type="italic">Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, according to the name of my god</hi>; for Nebuchadnezzar, by the addition of a name of honour in commemoration of the celebrated god of the kingdom, intended to show favour toward him, as also in the expression which follows, <hi type="italic">In whom is the spirit of the holy gods</hi>, which Nebuchadnezzar repeats in the address. But neither in the one nor the other of these considerations can we perceive the intention of specially captivating and appeasing the Jew Daniel; - not in the latter of these expressions, for two reasons: 1. because Nebuchadnezzar uses the expression not merely in the address to Daniel, but also in the references to him which go before; had he designed it to captivate him, he would have used these words of honour only in the address to him; 2. because the expression, “in whom is the spirit of the holy gods,” is so truly heathenish, that the Jew, who knew only <hi type="italic">one</hi> God, could not feel himself specially flattered by having the spirit of the holy gods ascribed to him. <div eID="gen15584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15585" type="x-p"/> If Nebuchadnezzar had had the intention of gaining the favour of Daniel, he would certainly, according to his confession (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.47">Dan 2:47</reference>), have attributed to him the spirit of the God of gods, the Lord of lords, - a confession which even as a heathen he could utter. We cannot give the king so little credit for understanding as to suppose that he meant to show<note placement="foot">Calvin here rightly remarks: <hi type="italic">non dubium est, quin hoc nomen graviter vulneraverit animum prophetae</hi>.</note> a special favour to Daniel, who held so firmly the confession of his father’s God, by reminding him that he had given him the name Belteshazzar after the name of his god Bel, whom the Jews abhorred as an idol. Thus the reminding him of this name, as well as the saying that he possessed the spirit of the holy gods, is not accounted for by supposing that he intended to appease and captivate Daniel. In showing the unsatisfactoriness of this interpretation of these expressions, we have set aside also the explanation of the reason, which is based upon it, why Daniel was called in to the king only after the Chaldean wise men; and other weighty considerations can also be adduced against it. First, the edict contains certainly nothing which can give room to the conjecture that Nebuchadnezzar entertained no true confidence, but much rather want of confidence, in him. The comparison of Nebuchadnezzar also with king Ahab in his conduct toward the prophet Micah is not suitable, because Ahab was not a mere polytheist as Nebuchadnezzar, but much rather, like Antiochus Epiphanes, persecuted the servants of Jehovah in his kingdom, and at the instigation of his heathenish wife Jezebel wished to make the worship of Baal the only religion of his kingdom. Finally, the relation of the dream does not indicate that Nebuchadnezzar, if he knew or suspected that the dream referred to himself as ruler over the whole earth, thought that he would come to ruin because of the God of the Jews. For that this does not follow from v. 14 (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.17">Dan 4:17</reference>), is shown not only by the divine visitation that happened to the king, as mentioned in v. 27 (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.30">Dan 4:30</reference>) in fulfilment of the dream, but also by the exhortation to the king with which Daniel closes the interpretation, “to break off sin by righteousness, and his iniquities by showing mercy to the poor” (v. 24 [v. 27]). <div eID="gen15585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15586" type="x-p"/> Thus there only remains this supposition, that the former revelations of God to the king had passed away from his heart and his memory; which was not surprising in the successful founder and ruler of a world-kingdom, if we consider that from twenty-five to thirty years must have passed away since Daniel interpreted to him his dream in the second year of his reign, and from ten to fifteen had passed since the miracle of the deliverance of the three from the burning fiery furnace. But if those earlier revelations of God were obscured in his heart by the fulness of his prosperity, and for ten years Daniel had no occasion to show himself to him as a revealer of divine secrets, then it is not difficult to conceive how, amid the state of disquietude into which the dream recorded in this chapter had brought him, he only gave the command to summon all the wise men of Babylon without expressly mentioning their president, so that they came to him first, and Daniel was called only when the natural wisdom of the Chaldeans had shown itself helpless. <div eID="gen15586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15587" type="x-p"/> The naming of Daniel by his Hebrew name in the manifesto, intended for all the people of the kingdom as well as for the Jews, is simply intended, as in <reference osisRef="Dan.2.29">Dan 2:29</reference>, to designate the interpreter of the dream, as distinguished from the native wise men of Babylon, as a Jew, and at the same time as a worshipper of the most high God; and by the addition, “whose name is Belteshazzar, according to the name of my god,” Nebuchadnezzar intends to indicate that Daniel by this name was brought into fellowship with his chief god Bel, and that not only as a worshipper of the God of the Jews, but also of the great god Bel, he had become a partaker of the spirit of the holy gods. But by the holy gods Nebuchadnezzar does not understand Jehovah, the Holy One, deriving this predicate “holy,” as M. Geier says, <hi type="italic">ex theologia Israëlitica</hi>, and the plur. “gods” denoting, as Calovius supposes, the <hi type="italic">mysterium pluralitatis personarum</hi>; but he speaks of the holy gods, as Jerome, Calvin, and Grotius supposed, as a heathen (<hi type="italic">ut idololatra</hi>) in a polytheistic sense. For that the revelation of supernatural secrets belonged to the gods, and that the man who had this power must possess the spirit of the gods, all the heathen acknowledged. Thus Pharaoh (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.38">Gen 41:38</reference>) judged regarding Joseph, and thus also the Chaldeans say to Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.11">Dan 2:11</reference>) that only the gods could know his dream. The truth lying at the foundation of this belief was acknowledged by Joseph before Pharaoh, as also by Daniel before the Chaldean king, for both of them declared before the heathen kings that the interpretation of their dreams was not in the power of man, but could come only from God (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.16">Gen 41:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.28">Dan 2:28</reference>). But when in the case before us Nebuchadnezzar speaks of the <hi type="italic">holy</hi> gods, he means by the expression the ἀγαθοδαίμονες as opposed to the κακοδαίμονες, using the word <hi type="italic">holy</hi> of the good gods, probably from his conversation with Daniel on the subject. <div eID="gen15587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15588" type="x-p"/> In the address, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.6">Dan 4:6</reference>, he calls Belteshazzar חרטמּיּא רב, <hi type="italic">master of the magicians</hi>, probably from the special branch of Chaldean wisdom with which Daniel was particularly conversant, at the same time that he was chief president over all the magicians. אנס, to oppress, to compel any one, to do violence to him; here, <hi type="italic">to make trouble, difficulty</hi>.
entries.98b968a2675f7adf48bb2b7f332a983d59ab37cb: <reference osisRef="Dan.4.10-Dan.4.11">Dan 4:10-11</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:7-8) <div eID="gen15588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15589" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar in these verses tells his dream. The first part of v. 10 is an absolute nominal sentence: <hi type="italic">the visions of my head lying upon my bed, then I saw</hi>, etc. - <hi type="italic">A tree stood in the midst of the earth</hi>. Although already very high, yet it became always the greater and the stronger, so that it reached eve unto heaven and was visible to the ends of the earth. V. 11. The perf. רבה and תּקיף express not its condition, but its increasing greatness and strength. In the second hemistich the imperf. ימטא, as the form of the striving movement, corresponds to them. Daniel B. Michaelis properly remarks, that Nebuchadnezzar saw the tree gradually grow and become always the stronger. חזות, <hi type="italic">the sight, visibleness</hi>. Its visibility reached unto the ends of the earth. The lxx have correctly ἡ ὅρασις αὑτοῦ; so the Vulgate; while Theodotion, with τὸ κύτος αὐτοῦ, gives merely the sense, its <hi type="italic">largeness</hi>, or <hi type="italic">dome</hi>. Hitzig altogether improperly refers to the Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥawzah</hi>; for <hi type="italic">ḥwzh</hi>, from <hi type="italic">ḥwz</hi>, corresponds neither with the Hebr. חזה, nor does it mean <hi type="italic">extent</hi>, but <hi type="italic">comprehension, embracing, enclosure</hi>, according to which the meanings, <hi type="italic">tractus, latus, regio</hi>, given in the Arab. Lex., are to be estimated.
entries.4ec780c0270a482ac1438ce21d77433f36667a67: <reference osisRef="Dan.4.12">Dan 4:12</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:9) <div eID="gen15589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15590" type="x-p"/> At the same time the tree abounded with leaves and fruit, so that birds and beasts found shadow, protection, and nourishment from it. שׁגיא, neither <hi type="italic">great</hi> nor <hi type="italic">many</hi>, but <hi type="italic">powerful</hi>, expressing the quantity and the greatness of the fruit. The בּהּ the Masoretes have rightly connected with לכלּא, to which it is joined by Maqqeph. The meaning is not: food was in it, the tree had food for all (Häv., Maur., and others), but: (it had) <hi type="italic">food for all in it</hi>, i.e., dwelling within its district (Kran., Klief.). The words, besides, do not form an independent sentence, but are only a further view of the שׁגיא (Kran.), and return in the end of the verse into further expansion, while the first and the second clauses of the second hemistich give the further expansion of the first clause in the verse. אטלל, <hi type="italic">umbram captavit</hi>, <hi type="italic">enjoyed the shadow</hi>; in Targg. The Aphel has for the most part the meaning <hi type="italic">obumbravit</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Kethiv</hi> ידרוּן is not to be changed, since the צפּרין is <hi type="italic">gen. comm</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> is conform to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Dan.4.18">Dan 4:18</reference></hi>, where the word is construed as fem. The expression <hi type="italic">all flesh</hi> comprehends the beasts of the field and the fowls of heaven, but is chosen with reference to men represented under this image. For the tree, mighty, reaching even to the heavens, and visible over the whole earth, is an easily recognised symbol of a world-ruler whose power stretches itself over the whole earth. The description of the growth and of the greatness of the tree reminds us of the delineation of Pharaoh and his power under the figure of a mighty cedar of Lebanon, cf. Eze 31:3., also Eze 17:22., Eze 19:10. The comparison of the growth of men to the growth of the trees is every frequent in biblical and other writings.
entries.328847c1e4b3d315720ff7b4873bf7c1948e5228: <reference osisRef="Dan.4.13">Dan 4:13</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:10) <div eID="gen15590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15591" type="x-p"/> By the words “I saw,” etc., a new incident of the dream is introduced. “A watcher and an holy one came down from heaven.” וקדּישׁ with the explic. ,ו <hi type="italic">even, and that too</hi>, brings it before us in a very expressive way that the עיר was an “holy one.” עיר is not to be combined with ציר, a messenger, but is derived from עוּר, to watch, and corresponds with the Hebr. ער, Sol 5:2; Mal 2:12, and signifies not keeping watch, but <hi type="italic">being watchful</hi>, one who is awake, as the scholium to the εἴρ of Theodotion in the Cod. Alex. explains it: ἐγρήγορος καὶ ἄγρυπνος. Similarly Jerome remarks: “<hi type="italic">significat angelos, quod semper vigilent et ad Dei imperium sint parati</hi>.” From this place is derived the name of ἐγρήγορος for the higher angels, who watch and slumber not, which is found in the book of Enoch and in other apocryphal writings, where it is used of good and of bad angels or demons. The designation of the angel as עיר is peculiar to this passage in the O.T. This gives countenance to the conjecture that it is a word associated with the Chaldee doctrine of the gods. Kliefoth quite justly, indeed, remarks, that this designation does not come merely from the lips of Nebuchadnezzar, but is uttered also by the holy watcher himself (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.14">Dan 4:14</reference>), as well as by Daniel; and he draws thence the conclusion, that obviously the holy watcher himself used this expression first of himself and the whole council of his companions, that Nebuchadnezzar used the same expression after him (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.10">Dan 4:10</reference>), and that Daniel again adopted it from Nebuchadnezzar. Thence it follows that by the word angel we are not to understand a heathen deity; for as certainly as, according to this narrative, the dream was given to Nebuchadnezzar by God, so certainly was it a messenger of God who brought it. But from this it is not to be concluded that the name accords with the religious conceptions of Nebuchadnezzar and of the Babylonians. Regarding the Babylonian gods Diod. Sic. ii. 30, says: “Under the five planets (= gods) are ranked thirty others whom they call the counselling gods (θεοὶ βούλαιοι), the half of whom have the oversight of the regions under the earth, and the other half oversee that which goes on on the earth, and among men, and in heaven. Every ten days one of these is sent as a messenger of the stars from the upper to the lower, and at the same time also one from the lower to the upper regions.” <div eID="gen15591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15592" type="x-p"/> If, according to <reference osisRef="Dan.4.14">Dan 4:14</reference>, the עירין constitute a deliberative council forming a resolution regarding the fate of men, and then one of these עירין comes down and makes known the resolution to the king, the conclusion is tenable that the עירין correspond to the θεοὶ βούλαιοι of the Babylonians. The divine inspiration of the dream corresponds with this idea. The correct thought lay at the foundation of the Chaldean representation of the θεοὶ βούλαιοι, that the relation of God to the world was mediate through the instrumentality of heavenly beings. The biblical revelation recognises these mediating beings, and calls them messengers of God, or angels and holy ones. Yea, the Scripture speaks of the assembling of angels before the throne of God, in which assemblies God forms resolutions regarding the fate of men which the angels carry into execution; cf. Job 1:6., 1Ki 22:19., <reference osisRef="Ps.89.8">Psa 89:8</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.7">7</reference>). Accordingly, if Nebuchadnezzar’s dream came from God, we can regard the עיר as an angel of God who belonged to the קדשׁים סוד around the throne of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.8">Psa 89:8</reference>). But this angel announced himself to the Chaldean king not as a messenger of the most high God, not as an angel in the sense of Scripture, but he speaks (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.14">Psa 89:14</reference>) of עירין גּזרת, of a resolution of the watchers, a <hi type="italic">fatum</hi> of the θεοὶ βούλαιοι who have the oversight of this world. The conception עירין גּזרת is not biblical, but Babylonian heathen. According to the doctrine of Scripture, the angels do not determine the fate of men, but God alone does, around whom the angels stand as ministering spirits to fulfil His commands and make known His counsel to men. The angel designates to the Babylonian king the divine resolution regarding that judgment which would fall upon him from God to humble him for his pride as “the resolution of the watchers,” that it might be announced to him in the way most easily understood by him as a divine judgment. On the other hand, one may not object that a messenger of God cannot give himself the name of a heathen deity, and that if Nebuchadnezzar had through misunderstanding given to the bringer of the dream the name of one of his heathen gods, Daniel ought, in interpreting the dream, to have corrected the misunderstanding, as Klief. says. For the messenger of God obviated this misunderstanding by the explanation that the matter was a decree of the watchers, to acknowledge the living God, that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whomsoever He will (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.17">Dan 4:17</reference>), whereby he distinctly enough announces himself as a messenger of the Most High, i.e., of the living God. To go yet further, and to instruct the king that his religious conceptions of the gods, the עירין, or θεοὶ βούλαιοι, were erroneous, inasmuch as, besides the Highest, the only God, there are no other gods, but only angels, who are no θεοί, but creatures of God, was not at all necessary fore the purpose of his message. This purpose was only to lead Nebuchadnezzar to an acknowledgment of the Most High, i.e., to an acknowledgment that the Most High rules as King of heaven over the kingdom of men. Now, since this was declared by the messenger of God, Daniel in interpreting the dream to the king needed to say nothing more than what he said in vv. 21, 22 (24, 25), where he designates the matter as a resolution of the Most High, and thereby indirectly corrects the view of the king regarding the “resolutions of the watchers,” and gives the king distinctly to understand that the humiliation announced to him was determined,<note placement="foot">We must altogether reject the assertion of Berth., v. Leng., Hitz., and Maur., that the language of this verse regarding the angel sent to Nebuchadnezzar is formed in accordance with the Persian representation of the seven Amschaspands (<hi type="italic">Amēschȧ - cpenta</hi>), since, according to the judgment of all those most deeply conversant with Parsism, the doctrine of the <hi type="italic">Amēschȧ - cpenta</hi> does not at all occur in the oldest parts of the Avesta, and the Avesta altogether is not so old as that the Babylonian doctrine of the gods can be shown to be dependent on the Zend doctrine of the Parsees.</note> not by the θεοὶ βούλαιοι of the Babylonians, but by the only true God, whom Daniel and his people worshipped. For Nebuchadnezzar designates עיר as קדּישׁ in the same sense in which, in <reference osisRef="Dan.4.5">Dan 4:5</reference>, he speaks of the holy gods.
entries.03991eb3098e9a1186f416cb7066555cc7623856: <reference osisRef="Dan.4.14-Dan.4.15">Dan 4:14-15</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:11-12) <div eID="gen15592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15593" type="x-p"/> The messenger of God cried with might (cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.3.4">Dan 3:4</reference>), “as a sign of the strong, firm utterance of a purpose” (Kran.). The command, Hew it down, is not given to the angels (Häv., Hitz., Auberl.). The plur. here is to be regarded as impersonal: <hi type="italic">the tree shall be cut down</hi>. אתּרוּ stands for אתּרוּ according to the analogy of the verbs 3rd <hi type="italic">gutt</hi>., from נתד, <hi type="italic">to fall off</hi>, spoken of withering leaves. In consequence of the destruction of the tree, the beasts which found shelter under it and among its branches flee away. Yet the tree shall not be altogether destroyed, but its stock (v. 12 15) shall remain in the earth, that it may again afterwards spring up and grow into a tree. The stem is not the royalty, the dynasty which shall remain in the house of Nebuchadnezzar (Häv.), but the tree with its roots is Nebuchadnezzar, who shall as king be cut down, but shall as a man remain, and again shall grow into a king. But the stock must be bound “with a band of iron and brass.” With these words, to complete which we must supply שׁבקוּ from the preceding context, the language passes from the type to the person represented by it. This transition is in the last part of the verse: <hi type="italic">with the beasts of the field let him have his portion in the grass of the earth</hi>; for this cannot be said of the stock with the roots, therefore these words are in the interpretation also (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.22">Dan 4:22</reference> [25]) applied directly to Nebuchadnezzar. But even in the preceding passages this transition is not doubtful. Neither the words <hi type="italic">in the grass of the field</hi>, nor the <hi type="italic">being wet with the dew of heaven</hi>, are suitable as applied to the stock of the tree, because both expressions in that case would affirm nothing; still less is <hi type="italic">the band of iron and brass</hi> congruous, for the trunk of a tree is not wont to be surrounded with bands of iron in order to prevent its being rent in pieces and completely destroyed. Thus the words refer certainly to Nebuchadnezzar; but the fastening in brass and iron is not, with Jerome and others, to be understood of the binding of the madman with chains, but figuratively or spiritually of the withdrawal of free self-determination through the fetter of madness; cf. The <hi type="italic">fetters of affliction</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.10">Psa 107:10</reference>; Job 36:8. With this fettering also agrees the going forth under the open heaven among the grass of the field, and the being wet with the dew of heaven, without our needing thereby to think of the maniac as wandering about without any oversight over him.
entries.3235be99e22905d12d56c187541cfac4e93fe71c: <reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Dan 4:16</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:13) <div eID="gen15593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15594" type="x-p"/> Here the angel declares by what means Nebuchadnezzar shall be brought into this condition. His heart shall be changed from a man’s heart, according to the following passage, into the heart of a beast. מן שׁנּא, <hi type="italic">to change, to make different from</hi>, so that it is no longer what it was. The <hi type="italic">Kethiv</hi> אנושׁא is the Hebr. form for the Chald. אנששׁא of the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, here, as in v. 14, where along with it also stands the Hebr. plur. form אנשׁים. אנושׁא stands here for the abbreviated comparison frequent in Hebr., אנושׁא מן לבב, and the 3rd <hi type="italic">pers. plur.</hi> ישׁנּון impers. for the passive. לבב is <hi type="italic">the heart</hi>, the centre of the intelligent soul-life. The heart of man is dehumanized when his soul becomes like that of a beast; for the difference between the heart of a man and that of a beast has its foundation in the difference between the soul of a man and the soul of a beast (Delitzsch, <hi type="italic">bibl. Psych</hi>. p. 252). <hi type="italic">And seven times shall pass over him</hi>, viz., during the continuance of the circumstances described; i.e., his condition of bondage shall last for seven times. Following the example of the lxx and of Josephus, many ancient and recent interpreters, down to Maur., Hitz., and Kran., understood by the word עדּנין <hi type="italic">years</hi>, because the <hi type="italic">times</hi> in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Dan 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">Dan 12:7</reference>, are also years, and because in <reference osisRef="Dan.4.29">Dan 4:29</reference> mention is made of twelve months, and thereby the <hi type="italic">time</hi> is defined as one year. But from <reference osisRef="Dan.4.29">Dan 4:29</reference> the duration of the עדּנין cannot at all be concluded, and in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Dan 7:25</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">Dan 12:7</reference> the times are not years. עדּן designates generally a definite period of time, whose length or duration may be very different. Seven is the “measure and signature of the history of the development of the kingdom of God, and of all the factors and phenomena significant for it” (Lämmert’s “Revision of the biblical Symbolical Numbers” in the <hi type="italic">Jahrbb.f. deutsche Theol</hi>. ix. p. 11); or as Leyrer, in Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Realencykl</hi>. xviii. p. 366, expresses himself, “the signature for all the actions of God, in judgment and in mercy, punishments, expiations, consecrations, blessings, connected with the economy of redemption, perfecting themselves in time.” Accordingly, “seven times” is the duration of the divine punishment which was decreed against Nebuchadnezzar for purposes connected with the history of redemption. Whether these times are to be understood as years, months, or weeks, is not said, and cannot at all be determined. The supposition that they were seven years “cannot well be adopted in opposition to the circumstance that Nebuchadnezzar was again restored to reason, a thing which very rarely occurs after so long a continuance of psychical disease” (J. B. Friedreich<hi type="italic">, Zur Bibel. Naturhist., anthrop. u. med. Fragmente</hi>, i. p. 316).
entries.4f208d50508a40f32f7a377e2da9ad56eb759c84: <reference osisRef="Dan.4.17">Dan 4:17</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:14) <div eID="gen15594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15595" type="x-p"/> The divine messenger concludes his announcement with the words that the matter was unchangeably decreed, for this purpose, that men might be led to recognise the supremacy of the Most High over the kings of the earth. The first two passages have no verb, and thus the <hi type="italic">verb. substant</hi>. must be supplied. Accordingly we must not translate: <hi type="italic">by the decree of the watchers is the message</hi>, i.e., is it delivered (Kran.), nor: <hi type="italic">the decree is included in the fate</hi>, <hi type="italic">the unalterable will of Heaven</hi> (Häv.); but  בdenotes the department within which the גּזרה lies, and is to be translated: “<hi type="italic">the message consists in</hi>, or <hi type="italic">rests on, the decree of the watchers</hi>.” גּזרה, the unchangeable decision, the <hi type="italic">decretum divinum, quod homini aut rebus humanis tanquam inevitabile impositum est</hi> (Buxtorf’s <hi type="italic">Lex. talm. rabb</hi>. p. 419), the <hi type="italic">Fatum</hi> in which the Chaldeans believed. Regarding פּתגּם see under Dan 3:16. Here the fundamental meaning, <hi type="italic">the message, that which is to happen</hi>, can be maintained. The second member is synonymous, and affirms the same thing in another way. The word, the utterance of the holy ones, i.e., the watchers (see under <reference osisRef="Dan.4.13">Dan 4:13</reference>), is שׁאלתּא, <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">matter</hi>. The meaning lying in the etymon, <hi type="italic">request</hi> or <hi type="italic">question</hi>, is not here suitable, but only the derivative meaning, <hi type="italic">matter</hi> as the object of the request or inquiry. The thing meant is that which is decided regarding the tree, that it should be cut down, etc. This is so clear, that a pronoun referring to it appears superfluous. דּי דּברת עד, <hi type="italic">till the matter that ... to the end that; not</hi> = דּי עד, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.25">Dan 4:25</reference>, because here no defining of time goes before. The changing of עד into על (Hitz.) is unnecessary and arbitrary. <hi type="italic">That the living may know, etc.</hi> The expression is general, because it is not yet said who is to be understood by the tree which should be cut down. This general expression is in reality correct; for the king comes by experience to this knowledge, and so all will attain to it who consider this. The two last passages of <reference osisRef="Dan.4.14">Dan 4:14</reference> express more fully how the Most High manifests His supremacy over the kingdom of men. The <hi type="italic">Kethiv</hi> עליה is shortened from עליהא, and in the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> is yet further shortened by the rejection of the ;י cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.5.21">Dan 5:21</reference>; Dan 7:4., etc.
entries.a4a18e7e304dd9523bd04dfb49416c88f625e827: <reference osisRef="Dan.4.18">Dan 4:18</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:15) <div eID="gen15595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15596" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar adds to his communication of his dream a command to Daniel to interpret it. The form פּשׁרא (<hi type="italic">its interpretation</hi>) is the old orthography and the softened form for פּשׁרהּ (cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.4.6">Dan 4:6</reference>).
entries.4569cdfc72f4ccb6604885a60c3a7476ee3db02d: <reference osisRef="Dan.4.19-Dan.4.27">Dan 4:19-27</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:16-24)<hi type="italic">The interpretation of the dream</hi>. <div eID="gen15596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15597" type="x-p"/> As Daniel at once understood the interpretation of the dream, he was for a moment so astonished that he could not speak for terror at the thoughts which moved his soul. This amazement seized him because he wished well to the king, and yet he must now announce to him a weighty judgment from God. <div eID="gen15597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15598" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Dan.4.19">Daniel 4:19</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:16) <div eID="gen15598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15599" type="x-p"/> The punctuation אשׁתּומם for אשׁתּומם is Syriac, as in Hebrew_Bible_8:27; cf. Winer’s <hi type="italic">Chald. Gram</hi>. §25, 2. חדא  כּשׁעהmeans, not <hi type="italic">about an hour</hi> (Mich., Hitz., Kran., etc.), but <hi type="italic">as it were an instant, a moment</hi>. Regarding שׁעה, see under Dan 3:6. The king perceives the astonishment of Daniel, and remarks that he has found the interpretation. Therefore he asks him, with friendly address, to tell him it without reserve. Daniel then communicates it in words of affectionate interest for the welfare of the king. The words, <hi type="italic">let the dream be to thine enemies</hi>, etc., do not mean: <hi type="italic">it is a dream, a prophecy, such as the enemies of the king might ungraciously wish</hi> (Klief.), but: <hi type="italic">may the dream with its interpretation be to thine enemies, may it be fulfilled to them or refer to them</hi> (Häv., Hitz., etc.). The <hi type="italic">Kethiv</hi> מראי is the regular formation from מרא with the suffix, for which the Masoretes have substituted the later Talmudic-Targ. form מר. With regard to שׂנאיך with the a shortened, as also השׁחין (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.16">Dan 3:16</reference>) and other participial forms, cf. Winer, <hi type="italic">Chald. Gram</hi>. §34, III. That Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Dan 4:16</reference>) in his account speaks in the third person does not justify the conclusion, either that another spake of him, and that thus the document is not genuine (Hitz.), nor yet the conclusion that this verse includes an historical notice introduced as an interpolation into the document; for similar forms of expression are often found in such documents: cf. Ezr 7:13-15; <reference osisRef="Esth.8.7">Est 8:7</reference>-8. <div eID="gen15599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15600" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Dan.4.20">Daniel 4:20</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:17) <div eID="gen15600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15601" type="x-p"/> Daniel interprets to the king his dream, repeating only here and there in an abbreviated form the substance of it in the same words, and then declares its reference to the king. With vv. Hebrew_Bible_17 (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.20">Dan 4:20</reference>) and Hebrew_Bible_18  (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.21">Dan 4:21</reference>) cf. vv. Hebrew_Bible_8 (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.11">Dan 4:11</reference>) and Hebrew_Bible_9 (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.12">Dan 4:12</reference>). The fuller description of the tree is subordinated to the relative clause, <hi type="italic">which thou hast seen</hi>, so that the subject is connected by הוּא (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.19">Dan 4:19</reference>), representing the <hi type="italic">verb. subst</hi>., according to rule, with the predicate אילנא. The interpretation of the separate statements regarding the tree is also subordinated in the relative clauses to the subject. For the <hi type="italic">Kethiv</hi> רבית = רביתּ, the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> gives the shortened form רבת, with the elision of the third radical, analogous to the shortening of the following מטת for מטת. To the call of the angel to “cut down the tree,” etc. (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.20">Dan 4:20</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.4.10-Dan.4.13">Dan 4:10-13</reference>), Daniel gives the interpretation, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.24">Dan 4:24</reference>, “This is the decree of the Most High which is come upon the king, that he shall be driven from men, and dwell among the beasts,” etc. על מטא = Hebr. על בּוא. The indefinite plur. form טרדין stands instead of the passive, as the following לך יטעמוּן and מצבּעין, cf. under Dan 3:4. Thus the subject remains altogether indefinite, and one has neither to think on men who will drive him from their society, etc., nor of angels, of whom, perhaps, the expulsion of the king may be predicated, but scarcely the feeding on grass and being wet with dew. <div eID="gen15601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15602" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Dan.4.26">Daniel 4:26</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:23) <div eID="gen15602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15603" type="x-p"/> In this verse the emblem and its interpretation are simply placed together, so that we must in thought repeat the פשׁרא דּנה from <reference osisRef="Dan.4.12">Dan 4:12</reference> before מלכוּתך. קיּמא, קאם do not in this place mean <hi type="italic">to stand, to exist, to remain</hi>, for this does not agree with the following דּי-nim; for until Nebuchadnezzar comes to the knowledge of the supremacy of God, his dominion shall not continue, but rest, be withdrawn. קוּם, <hi type="italic">to rise up</hi>, has here an inchoative meaning, <hi type="italic">again rise up</hi>. To שׁלּיטין (<hi type="italic">do rule</hi>) there is to be added from Hebrew_Bible_4:22 (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.25">Dan 4:25</reference>) the clause, <hi type="italic">over the kingdom of men</hi>. From this passage we have an explanation of the use of שׁמיּא, <hi type="italic">heaven</hi>, for עלּיא, <hi type="italic">the Most High, God of heaven</hi>, whence afterwards arose the use of βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν for βασιλεία τοῦ Θεοῦ. <div eID="gen15603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15604" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Dan.4.27">Daniel 4:27</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_4:24) <div eID="gen15604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15605" type="x-p"/> Daniel adds to his interpretation of the dream the warning to the king to break off his sins by righteousness and mercy, so that his tranquillity may be lengthened. Daniel knew nothing of a heathen <hi type="italic">Fatum</hi>, but he knew that the judgments of God were directed against men according to their conduct, and that punishment threatened could only be averted by repentance; cf. Jer 18:7.; Jon 3:5.; Isa 38:1. This way of turning aside the threatened judgment stood open also for Nebuchadnezzar, particularly as the time of the fulfilment of the dream was not fixed, and thus a space was left for repentance. The counsel of Daniel is interpreted by Berth., Hitz., and others, after Theodotion, the Vulgate, and many Church Fathers and Rabbis, as teaching the doctrine of holiness by works held by the later Jews, for they translate it: <hi type="italic">redeem thy sins by well-doing</hi> (Hitz.: <hi type="italic">buy freedom from thy sins by alms</hi>), <hi type="italic">and thy transgressions by showing mercy to the poor</hi>.<note placement="foot">Theodot. translates: καὶ τὰς ἁμαρτίας σου ἐν ἐλεημοσύναις λύτρωσαι καὶ τὰς ἀδικίας σου ἐν οἰκτιρμοῖς πενήτων. The Vulg.: <hi type="italic">et peccata tua eleemosynis redime et iniquitates tuas misericordiis pauperum</hi>. Accordingly, the Catholic Church regards this passage as a <hi type="italic">locus classicus</hi> for the doctrine of the merit of works, against which the <hi type="italic">Apologia Conf. August</hi>. first set forth the right exposition.</note> <div eID="gen15605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15606" type="x-p"/> But this translation of the first passage is verbally false; for פּרק does not mean <hi type="italic">to redeem, to ransom</hi>, and צדקה does not mean <hi type="italic">alms</hi> or <hi type="italic">charity</hi>. פּרק means <hi type="italic">to break off, to break in pieces,</hi> hence <hi type="italic">to separate, to disjoin, to put at a distance</hi>; see under Gen. 21:40. And though in the Targg. פרק is used for גּאל, פּדה, <hi type="italic">to loosen, to unbind</hi>, of redeeming, ransoming of the first-born, an inheritance or any other valuable possession, yet this use of the word by no means accords with sins as the object, because sins are not goods which one redeems or ransoms so as to retain them for his own use. חטי פּרק can only mean <hi type="italic">to throw away sins, to set one’s self free from sins</hi>. צדקה nowhere in the O.T. means <hi type="italic">well-doing</hi> or <hi type="italic">alms</hi>. This meaning the self-righteous Rabbis first gave to the word in their writings. Daniel recommends the king to practise righteousness as the chief virtue of a ruler in contrast to the unrighteousness of the despots, as Hgstb., Häv., Hofm., and Klief. have justly observed. To this also the second member of the verse corresponds. As the king should practise righteousness toward all his subjects, so should he exercise mercy toward the oppressed, the miserable, the poor.
